entry.title: RUSTSEC-2026-0432: Vulnerability in codeq
entry.summary: `codeq`: decoding untrusted input can allocate memory from an unchecked length prefix (denial of service)
entry.content:
History ⋅ Edit ⋅ JSON (OSV)

RUSTSEC-2026-0432

codeq: decoding untrusted input can allocate memory from an unchecked length prefix (denial of service)

CVSS Vector
CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:L
Patched
  • >=0.6.3

Description

codeq is a serialization library whose Decode trait reads length-prefixed values. For String and Vec<u8>, the length-prefixed Decode implementations read a 4-byte big-endian length and allocate a buffer of that size before reading the payload. Because the declared length is taken straight from the input with no upper bound and no cross-check against the bytes actually available, a tiny input can force an allocation of up to ~4 GiB. Code that decodes untrusted data through codeq can therefore be made to spike memory use and be OOM-killed (CWE-400, uncontrolled resource consumption).

The affected path, in src/codec/impls/string_impl.rs:

impl Decode for String {
    fn decode<R: io::Read>(mut r: R) -> Result<Self, io::Error> {
        let len = r.read_u32::<BigEndian>()? as usize;
        let mut buf = vec![0; len];   // allocates `len` bytes up front
        r.read_exact(&mut buf)?; 
        String::from_utf8(buf).map_err(|e| io::Error::new(io::ErrorKind::InvalidData, e))
    }
}

Any code that decodes attacker-controlled bytes through codeq can be forcedcto allocate up to ~4 GiB per decode call from a 4-byte length prefix. On a service decoding untrusted input this is a cheap denial of service (crash / OOM-kill). The practical severity depends on how the embedding wires codeq to untrusted bytes.

Remediation

Fixed in 0.6.3, which grows the decode buffers as payload bytes actually arrive instead of pre-allocating the full declared length (commit 9f15313, "fix: codec: grow decode buffers as payload bytes arrive"). Upgrade to codeq >= 0.6.3.

Advisory available under CC0-1.0 license.

Description

With Options::ENABLE_WIKILINKS, handle_wikilink builds a wikilink's target from the raw text of its body: scan_wikilink_pipe walks it looking for |, then contains('\0') and from_replace_nuls walk it again. Once a wikilink is created, disable_all_links only disables Link entries, so every enclosing ![[ stays live on the wikilink stack. On ![[![[![[…]]]]]] each of those openers then resolves in turn and rescans everything inside it, which is quadratic in the nesting depth. The event count stays tiny, because in the unpiped case each enclosing image replaces its body with a fresh text node, so all of that work is thrown away.

Applications that parse untrusted Markdown with ENABLE_WIKILINKS set, including through Options::all(), are affected. The option is off by default. Parsing without it is not affected.

The flaw was fixed in #1186 and released in 0.13.6.

Description

ZipArchive::extract() sizes the symlink-target buffer from the uncompressed size declared in the central directory record, before reading a single byte of entry data:

let mut target = Vec::with_capacity(file.size() as usize);

Both inputs are attacker-controlled. ZipFile::size() returns uncompressed_size verbatim from the central directory, widened to a full u64 by a ZIP64 extended-information extra field, and is never cross-checked against the compressed size, the remaining archive length, or any platform-appropriate bound for a symlink target. ZipFile::is_symlink() is decided entirely by the S_IFLNK bit of the external-attributes field.

Vec::with_capacity() is infallible: when the reservation is refused it calls handle_alloc_error() and aborts the process. This is not a Rust panic. It is not caught by catch_unwind(), is unaffected by panic = "unwind", and is not contained by running the call on a worker thread.

A 112-byte archive is sufficient. One Stored entry flagged S_IFLNK with a ZIP64 field declaring uncompressed_size = 2^62 and a zero-byte payload makes extract() fail with:

memory allocation of 4611686018427387904 bytes failed
Aborted (core dumped)          # exit 134

The declared value only needs to exceed the host's address space, not its RAM: Vec::with_capacity() maps address space without touching pages, so resident memory stays flat and the abort happens on the refused reservation itself. Under a ulimit -v cap or a memory-constrained container the threshold drops far enough that a plain 32-bit uncompressed_size with no ZIP64 field suffices.

Applications that extract archives from untrusted input are affected on Unix and Windows targets with default features and no special configuration: upload handling, mail-attachment processing, package and artefact ingestion, backup restore and container-image layer extraction. No confidentiality or integrity property is affected: there is no memory unsafety, no out-of-bounds access, no disclosure and no data corruption.

The fix landed in zip-rs/zip2#984 and shipped in 9.0.0.

For further details see: https://github.com/zip-rs/zip2/security/advisories/GHSA-q7v9-x93c-xqv3

Affected Functions
Version
ant_releases::AntReleaseRepoActions::extract_release_archive
  • <=0.4.3

Description

ant-releases downloads and unpacks release archives from the safe_network / autonomi repositories. When it extracts an archive, it builds each output path by joining the archive entry's own name onto the destination directory, with no check for .. or absolute components — a classic "zip-slip" path traversal (CWE-22 / CWE-23). A crafted archive can therefore create or overwrite files outside the intended extraction directory.

In extract_release_archive (src/lib.rs), the ZIP branch does:

let out_path = dest_dir_path.join(file.name());   // raw zip entry name, no containment check
if file.name().ends_with('/') {
    std::fs::create_dir_all(&out_path)?;          // dir created outside dest_dir
} else {
    let mut outfile = std::fs::File::create(&out_path)?;   // file written outside dest_dir
    std::io::copy(&mut file, &mut outfile)?;
}

Proof of concept

A one-entry ZIP whose entry name is ../foo_pwned.txt, passed to AntReleaseRepoActions::extract_release_archive (obtained via the crate's public <dyn AntReleaseRepoActions>::default_config()), writes foo_pwned.txt as a sibling of the destination directory, outside it. Confirmed against the published 0.4.3 crate.

CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:H/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:N
Patched
  • >=0.5.29
Affected Functions
Version
rio_vt::ansi::kitty_graphics_protocol::parse
  • <=0.5.28

Description

The Kitty graphics protocol handler in rio-vt builds a filesystem path from an attacker-controlled APC escape sequence and, for the temp-file medium, only checks that the path contains the substring "tty-graphics-protocol" before it opens, reads, and remove_files it. There is no .. rejection and no canonicalization, so a path containing the marker substring plus .. escapes the terminal's temp directory (path traversal, CWE-22/CWE-23).

Because a terminal renders whatever arrives on the PTY (ssh output, a cat'd file, CI logs), untrusted output can delete a file outside the temp area and cause its bytes to be read back in.

Details

The sink is create_graphic_data() in src/ansi/kitty_graphics_protocol.rs, in the TransmissionMedium::TempFile branch, reachable through the public API rio_vt::ansi::kitty_graphics_protocol::parse. The path is the base64 APC payload of an a=t,t=t command, and the guard is:

let path = Path::new(path_str);
if !path.is_file() { return Err(GraphicError::FileNotFound); }       // literal path, resolves `..`
// reject /proc/ /sys/ /dev/ (lowercased substring)
if cmd.medium == TransmissionMedium::TempFile
    && !path_str.contains("tty-graphics-protocol") {                 // SUBSTRING, not a component
    return Err(GraphicError::InvalidData);
}
// ...
let mut file = File::open(path)...;          // reads file bytes
if cmd.medium == TransmissionMedium::TempFile {
    let _ = std::fs::remove_file(path);      // deletes the file
}

This affects any terminal emulator or application built on rio-vt (e.g. the Rio terminal) that renders attacker-influenced output: an out-of-bounds file is deleted, and its contents are read into the process.

The fix

Fixed in rio-vt 0.5.29 (Rio 0.5.29) by PR #1998. For the temp-file medium the parent directory is resolved with canonicalize before any check, the resolved entry must lie inside a temp directory (temp_dir(), /tmp or /dev/shm) and contain the marker, and the delete goes through unlinkat on a handle to the validated directory, so neither .. nor a swapped symlink can redirect it. Path checks for the file medium also run on the file actually opened.

Advisory available under CC0-1.0 license.

Unaffected

Affected Functions
Version
evtx::wevt_templates::wevtcache::WevtCacheReader::next_entry
  • >=0.11.0, <0.15.1
evtx::wevt_templates::wevtcache::for_each_crim_blob
  • >=0.11.0, <0.15.1

Description

Affected versions of evtx did not bound a per-entry payload length read from a .wevtcache file before allocating a buffer sized from it, allowing a tiny crafted file to force a multi-gigabyte allocation and abort the process (out-of-memory denial of service, CWE-400).

Details

In WevtCacheReader::next_entry (src/wevt_templates/wevtcache.rs), the per-entry payload length is read as a u64 straight from the file and used to size a zeroing buffer before any data is read:

let len = usize::try_from(len_u64)?;   // u64 taken directly from the entry header
let mut buf = vec![0u8; len];          // unbounded allocation, sized from the file
reader.read_exact(&mut buf)?;          // only fails AFTER the allocation

The only check on len is that it fits in usize; there is no check that it fits within the bytes remaining in the file. An entry header declaring a ~4 GiB length therefore makes the crate request a ~4 GiB allocation from a file of only ~25 bytes.

The sink is reachable through the public API evtx::wevt_templates::wevtcache::for_each_crim_blob(path, f) (and the WevtCacheReader::next_entry it drives). The .wevtcache reader first shipped in 0.11.0, and every published version from 0.11.0 through 0.14.0 is affected. The code lives in the wevt_templates feature, which is enabled by default through the evtx_dump feature. The fix landed in 0.15.1: 0.15.0 was tagged but never published to crates.io (its Windows build failed), so 0.15.1 is the first patched release available. The Python bindings (evtx on PyPI) carry the fix as of 0.15.0.

Reproduction

A ~25-byte file is sufficient: the .wevtcache magic (WEVTCACH), a version (u32 LE) of 1, an entry_count (u32 LE) of 1, then one entry consisting of a kind byte and a len (u64 LE) set to a large value (e.g. 0xFFFFFFF0), with no payload bytes following. Passing that file to for_each_crim_blob triggers the oversized allocation before the short read fails.

Affected Functions
Version
nix_nar::Decoder::unpack
  • <0.6.0

Description

Decoder::unpack does not safely contain the paths it extracts, so a malicious NAR archive can create files outside the destination directory — a path traversal (CWE-22).

In src/dec.rs (Decoder::unpack):

  • A symlink entry's target is written without checking where it points (src/dec.rs:153), so the archive can create a symlink that escapes the destination directory.
  • The out-of-destination containment check compares path strings only and does not account for symlinks created earlier in the same unpack (src/dec.rs:176-181), before reaching the write sinks (std::fs::create_dir at src/dec.rs:201 and OpenOptions::open at src/dec.rs:218).
  • The parser also accepts entry names containing / (src/parser.rs:138-147).

Combined, a malicious archive can include a symlink a pointing at an external directory and then an entry named a/b, causing b to be written to <external>/b, outside the destination. This can create new files anywhere the process can write (it cannot overwrite existing files), which is escalatable to code execution by planting files in attacker-chosen locations.

Reported

References

Unaffected

Description

The build script of libz-sys version <= 1.1.30 prints the full environment of the build, including any secrets it contains, to its stdout when compiled with cc@1.6.0 or later on a Unix host. This affects any build that depends on libz-sys. Cargo saves build script stdout under target/, so the values end up in anything that stores or shares the target/ directory, such as CI caches.

This is similar to the Miri issue.

Details

To decide whether to link against a system zlib, the libz-sys build script compiles a small test program with a compiler command from cc and logs it with:

println!("running {:?}", cmd);

On Unix, Debug impl for std::process::Command prints every environment variable explicitly set on the command. Before cc@1.6.0, its Tool::to_command() set only a few compiler-specific variables. Starting with cc@1.6.0 (released 2026-10-03), Tool::to_command() clears the environment and sets every variable explicitly.

Cargo parses build script stdout for cargo: directives, and stores the full output in the build directory. It also prints it with -vv.

The probe runs for a default libz-sys build, including when pkg-config finds zlib, unless one of these applies:

  • the target is Windows, Android, Haiku or OpenHarmony
  • static linking is requested via the static feature or LIBZ_SYS_STATIC=1
  • the zlib-ng features are enabled without stock-zlib

Mitigations

Fixed in libz-sys@1.1.31, which no longer logs the probe command.

If you cannot upgrade, here are some workarounds:

  • Build with LIBZ_SYS_STATIC=1 or the static feature, which skips the probe.
  • Pin cc to a release before 1.6.0 (cargo update cc --precise <version>).

Note that upgrading libz-sys does not remove values already written. If an affected build already ran with secrets in its environment, clear CI caches and stored artifacts containing its target/build directory, and consider rotating those secrets.

Description

Summary

Nextest versions between 0.9.125 and 0.9.149 (inclusive) allow the cargo nextest run --rerun (or -R) command with a malicious portable recording to run arbitrary code during the build. The result is arbitrary code execution with the privileges of the user running cargo nextest.

This vulnerability requires that the experimental run recording functionality is enabled. An attacker can plausibly trick a victim into enabling this feature.

Details

Nextest's portable recordings contain build scope arguments. These arguments are deserialized verbatim from portable recordings, and are not validated. As a result, it is possible to construct an archive with a custom --config argument that causes Cargo to execute arbitrary code.

Nextest 0.9.150 records the build scope as structured data, and passes each value to Cargo joined to its flag (for example, --package=<value>), so a recording can no longer add other Cargo options.

Impact

A malicious portable recording leads to arbitrary code execution as the user who runs cargo nextest run --rerun, during the build phase, before any test runs.

  • The injected configuration takes effect during cargo build, so the payload is run even on a warm build cache, and even when no tests are ultimately executed. Inspecting the recorded tests (with e.g. cargo nextest replay) before running them does not help, since the code has already run by the time the tests would start.
  • Arbitrary code execution happens as the invoking user, without a prompt or trust warning. The only signal is a rerun: inheriting build scope… line. On CI, this includes access to whatever secrets are accessible to the job, including repository tokens and deployment credentials.
  • A malicious payload can invoke the real compiler afterwards, so the build and tests complete normally. The recording is otherwise a valid, ordinary recording.
  • The full Cargo --config surface is exposed. This includes build.rustc-wrapper, build.rustc, target.*.linker, target.*.runner, env.*, and patch.* and source.*.replace-with (redirecting dependencies to an attacker-controlled repository or registry).
  • The delivery mechanism matches the feature's intended use, since portable recordings are designed to be shared across machines. For example, an attacker could pose as a user asking a maintainer for help triaging their flaky test report. Because --rerun also accepts process substitution, cargo nextest run --rerun <(curl …) would fetch the recording directly from a URL.

Exploitation requires convincing the victim to run cargo nextest run --rerun against an attacker-supplied portable recording. The rerun feature is experimental and must be enabled, via e.g. NEXTEST_EXPERIMENTAL_RECORD=1.

Remediations

  • Upgrade cargo-nextest to version 0.9.150 or above.
  • In your repositories, set the minimum required version to 0.9.150. In .config/nextest.toml: 
    nextest-version = "0.9.150"
    This way, anyone who interacts with your repository will be notified to upgrade their version of nextest.
  • If you are using an affected version, do not enable the experimental run recording feature.

Credit

Reported by inanna-malick.

Reported

Type
Vulnerability

Keywords
#pam #authentication #ffi #undefined-behavior
References
  • https://github.com/lvkv/pam-rs/issues/16
Patched
  • >=0.1.2

Description

In affected versions, PamHandle::get_user can return Err(PAM_SUCCESS) after it gets the username successfully. PAM modules that return this "error" code from sm_authenticate or sm_acct_mgmt early-return a success code to PAM without doing any further verification. This means a user could log in when they shouldn't be able to (e.g., if the module is sufficient).

The pam_try! macro of this crate early-returns the code in this exact way:

fn sm_authenticate(pamh: &mut PamHandle, args: Vec<&CStr>, flags: PamFlag) -> PamResultCode {
    let user = pam_try!(pamh.get_user(None)); // Can return PAM_SUCCESS here.
    // If it does, the module does not get to this line.
}

The root cause is an incorrect FFI declaration for pam_get_user(3). This C function writes a pointer to the username through its user argument (of type const char **user). This crate's binding declared this argument as a shared reference (&*mut c_char). Writing through a shared reference is undefined behavior.

Thus, the compiler can assume that the local pointer, whose address is passed as user, is still null after the call. After the call, the affected code returns Ok only if the return code is PAM_SUCCESS and this pointer is not null. Otherwise, it returns the return code as an error. If the compiler assumes that the pointer is null, get_user returns an error even when the return code is PAM_SUCCESS. Release builds have been observed to do this. Debug builds usually work correctly, so tests in debug mode can miss the problem.

Version 0.1.2 changes the declaration to &mut *const c_char. The fix is in commit 401c961.

If a module cannot upgrade, do not return the error code from get_user. Return a failure code instead, for example pam_try!(pamh.get_user(None), PamResultCode::PAM_AUTH_ERR). This makes the module deny access instead of allowing it, but the undefined behavior remains.

This is controlled by PeerOptions::http_upstream_request_policy; HttpUpstreamRequestPolicy::preserve() restores the old passthrough behavior and should not be used if the origin relies on headers added by Pingora. Description

Log2Cache::new(n) fills its three tables with entries for 0..=n, but the three accessor methods index those tables with get_unchecked on a value the caller supplies. Nothing bounds the argument and nothing documents a bound, so any value above the n the cache was built with reads past the end of the vector. CountType is u32, so the read can land up to u32::MAX elements away, and plog2p() returns the value it read, disclosing whatever lies there.

For example, Log2Cache::new(4) builds tables holding 5 entries (indices 0,1,2,3,4). Then cache.nlog2n(60000) reads index 60000, far outside the allocation. Under AddressSanitizer this faults with SEGV; Miri reports it as undefined behavior at src/log2cache.rs:42.

nlog2n_difference() is off by one further: in the affected versions new(n) pushes n entries into that table rather than n + 1, so even nlog2n_difference(n) is out of bounds.

This can be triggered through safe public APIs — Log2Cache::new() and any of nlog2n(), nlog2n_difference() and plog2p() — with no unsafe required from the caller.

Description

OrderedSkipList, SkipSet and SkipMap can free a node that is still linked when a Comparator or Ord implementation gives different answers for the same pair of values during one mutating call. A later call reads the freed memory (CWE-416). A safe impl Ord with the default comparator is enough to reach it.

The mutating traversals record a precursor at each level: the last node whose link points at a node comparing not-Less than the target. The splice code assumes every recorded precursor's link points at or past the final position. If a later comparison reports one of those nodes as Less, the walk steps past it and the assumption breaks. Removals such as take_first, take and remove then rewire the wrong link and free the target while its real predecessor still points at it. insert builds crossed links and wrong skip distances from the same precursors.

A comparator that is a pure function of its two arguments cannot trigger this, even if it is not transitive. The trigger is a stateful or non-deterministic implementation, for example one that reads a counter, a cache, a clock or a random source.

The flaw was corrected in 1.3.0. The mutating traversals track the link target of the lowest recorded precursor and panic with "comparator does not implement a total order" when a Less answer contradicts an earlier one. Every splice site also checks its precursors before the first write. Each detected contradiction panics before any link, value or length changes, so the collection stays valid and safe to drop.

On wasm32, zstd-sys provides malloc and free to the C library through a shim over Rust's allocator. The shim did not check for allocation failure: it wrote its size header to address 0 and returned address 4, which the C library used as a valid buffer. free(NULL) also read below address 0.

Whenever the instance cannot grow its memory by what a frame asks for, a small crafted frame (a 9-byte header declaring a 128 MiB window is enough) made decompression write decoded data over the bottom of the module's linear memory, instead of failing. The corruption stays within the wasm sandbox.

The flaw was corrected by returning NULL on allocation failure or size overflow, and by making free(NULL) a no-op.

Description

When decompression fails inside a legacy (zstd v0.4 to v0.7) frame, the bundled zstd library reports the output buffer as fully written although nothing was written. DCtx::decompress_stream committed that position even on error, and for a Vec<u8> destination this extended the vector's length over uninitialized memory.

Legacy support is enabled by default. A 5- or 6-byte corrupt legacy frame is enough: through zstd::stream::write::Decoder, up to 32 KiB of stale heap memory is then passed to the wrapped writer on the next write() or flush(), or when an auto_flush()/on_flush() decoder is dropped. Whether this reaches an attacker depends on where the application sends the decompressed output. zstd::stream::read::Decoder, zstd::decode_all and the bulk API are not affected.

Before zstd-safe 4.0.0, output buffers could only be initialized slices. The zstd crate's own writer had the same flaw from 0.4.22 to 0.7.x, which is covered by a separate advisory.

The flaw was corrected by only committing the buffer positions of a successful call.
